blocks.text: A car's side window can be struck with a hammer and crumble into thousands of blunt pieces, yet the same thickness of ordinary annealed glass would break into a few dangerous daggers. The difference is not the composition but a deliberate residual stress put in by heat treatment. Ceramics for pumps, furnaces and knee implants are similarly chosen not by one number but by a balance of hardness, toughness and temperature capability.

blocks.markdown: **Glass** is an inorganic solid with no long-range crystal order: its silica network is amorphous. Because it has no sharp melting point, its viscosity increases continuously as it cools, and the properties change character over a narrow range of temperature called the glass transition. Engineering ceramics (alumina, silicon carbide, zirconia) are, in contrast, polycrystalline and crystalline, and are chosen for hardness and temperature resistance.

blocks.title: Glass transition temperature
blocks.text: The **glass transition temperature** $T_g$ is the temperature range, about 550 to 570 C for soda-lime glass (typical), at which a cooling melt changes from a viscous liquid to a rigid, brittle solid without crystallising. It appears as a change in slope of volume against temperature, and the viscosity at $T_g$ is of order $10^{12}$ Pa s. Above $T_g$ internal stresses can relax by viscous flow; below it they are frozen in.

blocks.markdown: **Thermal tempering.** Annealed glass has a surface that is nearly stress-free but is covered with small scratches. A tensile stress opens a scratch and the glass breaks at only about 40 to 50 MPa. Tempering puts the surface into compression so that an applied tensile load must first cancel the compression before any flaw feels tension. The process has four stages.

items: Heat the sheet to about 620 to 650 C, above $T_g$, so it is soft and stress-free.
Blast both faces with cold air jets so the surface cools quickly.
The surface contracts and becomes rigid (below $T_g$) while the interior is still hot and soft, so the interior can flow to accommodate the shrinking skin and no stress builds up yet.
The interior then cools and tries to contract, but the rigid outer skin resists. The skin is pushed into **compression** and the core is pulled into **tension**.

blocks.caption: The surface compression is balanced by core tension of about half its magnitude. The applied tensile stress at failure is increased by the surface compression, because it must first neutralise it.

blocks.title: Strength and core tension of tempered glass
blocks.prompt: A tempered glass plate has a surface compressive residual stress of 110 MPa. The annealed glass of the same composition and surface finish fails at 45 MPa. Estimate the applied tensile stress that breaks the tempered plate, and the magnitude of the tension in the core.

steps.text: Failure occurs when the applied tensile stress plus the residual stress equals the flaw-limited strength: $\sigma_{\text{applied}}-110=45$, so the applied stress must overcome the compression first.
The core tension for a parabolic stress profile is half the surface compression in magnitude.

blocks.answer: The tempered plate fails at about 155 MPa, 3.4 times the annealed strength, and has a core tension of about 55 MPa; if a crack penetrates the core, the stored energy shatters it into small blunt pieces.

blocks.markdown: **Why the three differ.** Silicon carbide, with a strongly covalent bond, is the hardest and keeps its strength to very high temperatures, and its high thermal conductivity helps thermal shock resistance. Alumina is the cheap general-purpose ceramic: hard, stiff, electrically insulating and chemically inert. Zirconia is tougher than the other two because of **transformation toughening**: the tetragonal grains near a crack tip transform to the larger monoclinic structure, which expands and squeezes the crack shut. This effect is lost at high temperature, so zirconia is limited to lower temperatures.

**Thermal shock.** A ceramic suddenly cooled at its surface by $\Delta T$ develops a surface tensile stress. Using an elastic constrained-contraction model, the stress is $\sigma=E\alpha\Delta T/(1-\nu)$, so the largest sudden temperature drop the part can withstand without fracture is obtained by setting this stress equal to the strength $\sigma_f$.

blocks.caption: sigma_f is the tensile strength, nu Poisson's ratio, E Young's modulus and alpha the linear thermal expansion coefficient. Larger strength, smaller E and smaller alpha all improve thermal shock resistance.

blocks.title: Thermal shock limit of an alumina tube
blocks.prompt: An alumina tube has $\sigma_f=300$ MPa, $\nu=0.22$, $E=380$ GPa and $\alpha=8\times10^{-6}$ K$^{-1}$ (typical). What is the largest sudden surface temperature drop it can survive?

steps.text: Divide to find the temperature drop.

blocks.answer: About 77 K: quenching alumina by more than about 77 K can crack it.

blocks.title: Selecting a ceramic
blocks.text: Wear and sliding: choose the hardest, SiC or alumina. Highest temperature and thermal shock: SiC (high thermal conductivity, low expansion), then alumina. Toughness and impact: toughened zirconia, at moderate temperature. Electrical insulation and low cost: alumina. Always check the strength scatter, thermal shock limit and the mounting (thermal expansion mismatch with a metal housing).

blocks.title: Ceramics fail without warning
blocks.text: None of these ceramics yields. Their strength depends on flaw size and scatters, and tempered glass cannot be cut or drilled after tempering because the stored energy releases. Use ceramics in compression where possible, avoid stress concentrations and sudden temperature changes, and design with a probabilistic safety margin.

points: Glass has no melting point: it passes through a glass transition at $T_g$ (about 550 to 570 C for soda-lime), above which stress relaxes by flow and below which it is frozen in.

Thermal tempering cools the surface first, leaving the surface in compression and the core in tension (about half in magnitude); the applied tensile stress at failure rises by the surface compression.

SiC is hardest and the most temperature-capable, alumina is the general-purpose insulating wear ceramic, and zirconia is the toughest but limited to lower temperature; thermal shock limit $\Delta T_{\text{crit}}=\sigma_f(1-\nu)/(E\alpha)$.

questions.stem: What best describes the glass transition of a silicate glass on cooling?

options.text: A sharp freezing at a fixed temperature, with the sudden formation of crystals
A transformation from a brittle solid to a ductile solid at a critical temperature
A gradual change from a viscous liquid to a rigid, brittle solid without crystallising, over a narrow temperature range
A temperature at which the glass becomes electrically conducting

questions.correctOptionText: A gradual change from a viscous liquid to a rigid, brittle solid without crystallising, over a narrow temperature range

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: crystallisation is not part of the glass transition; the glass stays amorphous.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: glass becomes more rigid, not more ductile, as it cools through the transition.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: viscosity rises continuously and the structure becomes frozen in while remaining amorphous.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: electrical conduction is not what defines the transition.

questions.explanation: A glass-forming liquid cools without crystallising, so its viscosity increases steadily until it is effectively a rigid solid. The change in slope of the volume-temperature curve at $T_g$ marks where viscous flow can no longer relax stress on the timescale of cooling.

questions.stem: In thermal tempering of glass, why does the surface end up in compression and the core in tension?

options.text: The surface hardens first while the core is still hot, and the core contracts later against the rigid skin
The surface cools more slowly than the core, so it contracts later
Cold air jets introduce compressive stress by chemical exchange of ions
The core crystallises and expands, pushing the surface into compression

questions.correctOptionText: The surface hardens first while the core is still hot, and the core contracts later against the rigid skin

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the delayed contraction of the core is resisted by the already rigid surface layers.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: the surface cools faster, not more slowly, since the air jets extract heat there.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: ion exchange is chemical strengthening, a different process.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: no crystallisation occurs in tempering.

questions.explanation: The air jets cool the surface through $T_g$ while the interior is still soft and can flow to accommodate the shrinkage. When the interior later cools and contracts, the rigid skin resists, leaving the skin in compression and the core in balancing tension.

questions.stem: Which of alumina, silicon carbide and zirconia has the highest fracture toughness at room temperature, and why?

options.text: Silicon carbide, because its hardness is greatest
Alumina, because its melting point is the highest
All three are equal, since ceramics are all brittle
Zirconia, because stress-induced tetragonal-to-monoclinic transformation near a crack tip closes the crack

questions.correctOptionText: Zirconia, because stress-induced tetragonal-to-monoclinic transformation near a crack tip closes the crack

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: hardness is not toughness; SiC is harder but its toughness is lower.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: melting point does not set the toughness.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: toughness differs widely among ceramics, with zirconia roughly double that of alumina.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: transformation toughening gives yttria-stabilised zirconia the highest toughness of the three.

questions.explanation: Tetragonal zirconia particles near a crack tip transform to the monoclinic form with an expansion of a few per cent, which squeezes the crack shut and absorbs energy. This raises the toughness to roughly 6 to 10 MPa m$^{1/2}$ against about 3.5 to 4.5 for alumina.

questions.stem: A furnace component must operate continuously at about 1500 C in air and experience repeated heating and cooling. Which ceramic is the best choice, and what is its key advantage?

options.text: Yttria-stabilised zirconia, because its toughness is highest at 1500 C
Silicon carbide, because it keeps its strength to high temperature and its high thermal conductivity and low expansion resist thermal shock
Soda-lime glass, because it is soft above its transition temperature
Alumina, because its thermal conductivity is the highest

questions.correctOptionText: Silicon carbide, because it keeps its strength to high temperature and its high thermal conductivity and low expansion resist thermal shock

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: zirconia's transformation toughening is lost and its strength falls at such temperatures.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: SiC combines high-temperature strength with good thermal shock resistance.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: soda-lime glass softens at about 550 to 570 C and would deform completely.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: alumina's conductivity is lower than that of silicon carbide and it has a larger expansion coefficient.

questions.explanation: SiC is hardest and strongest at high temperature, with a high thermal conductivity (80 to 120 W m$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$) and low expansion that give the best thermal shock resistance of the three. Zirconia loses its toughening and strength above roughly 1000 C.

questions.stem: A seal face in a pump handling an abrasive slurry at moderate temperature must resist sliding wear. Which ceramic is the best choice and what limit must the designer respect?

options.text: Zirconia, because it is the hardest, with no limits at all
Glass, because it has a very low density
Alumina, because it is soft and conforms to the shaft
Silicon carbide, being the hardest, with care over brittleness and thermal shock at start-up

questions.correctOptionText: Silicon carbide, being the hardest, with care over brittleness and thermal shock at start-up

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: zirconia is the least hard of the three and it has its own temperature limits.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: glass is much softer than the technical ceramics and has low wear resistance.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: alumina is hard, not soft; softness is not what is wanted here.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: hardness governs abrasive wear, and brittleness and thermal shock must still be respected.

questions.explanation: Abrasive wear resistance rises with hardness, so silicon carbide (about 25 to 28 GPa) is the usual choice for pump seal faces. Its limits are low toughness, so it must be loaded in compression and kept free of impacts, and its thermal shock resistance.

questions.stem: A tempered glass plate has a surface compressive residual stress of 98 MPa. The same glass annealed fails at 42 MPa under a tensile load. Estimate the applied tensile stress at which the tempered plate fails, in MPa.
questions.explanation: The applied tensile stress must first cancel the residual compression and then supply the flaw-limited strength, so $\sigma_{\text{fail}}=42+98=140$ MPa. This is about 3.3 times the annealed strength.

questions.stem: A thermally tempered glass pane has a surface compressive stress of 120 MPa. Assuming a parabolic through-thickness stress profile, find the magnitude of the tensile stress in the core of the pane, in MPa.
questions.explanation: For a parabolic profile in a plate, the forces balance when the core tension is half the surface compression in magnitude, so $\sigma_{\text{core}}=120/2=60$ MPa. This stored tension is why a break that reaches the core propagates widely and fragments the glass.

questions.stem: A silicon carbide nozzle has strength $\sigma_f=380$ MPa, Poisson's ratio $\nu=0.16$, Young's modulus $E=400$ GPa and thermal expansion coefficient $\alpha=4.3\times10^{-6}$ K$^{-1}$. Estimate the largest sudden temperature drop at the surface that it can survive, using $\Delta T_{\text{crit}}=\sigma_f(1-\nu)/(E\alpha)$, in K.
questions.explanation: Substituting in SI units, $\Delta T_{\text{crit}}=380\times10^{6}\times0.84/(400\times10^{9}\times4.3\times10^{-6})=3.19\times10^{8}/1.72\times10^{6}=186$ K. A sudden quench greater than about 186 K risks fracture.

questions.stem: Describe the glass transition and explain, step by step, how thermal tempering gives a glass plate compressive surface stress. State why a tempered plate is stronger than an annealed one and name one limitation of tempered glass.
markingGuide: Glass is amorphous with no sharp melting point; viscosity rises continuously, and at the glass transition $T_g$ it becomes a rigid, brittle solid
Heat above $T_g$ (soft, stress free) and then quench the surfaces with air
Surface cools through $T_g$ and becomes rigid while the interior is still soft and can accommodate the contraction
The interior then cools and contracts against the rigid skin, leaving the skin in compression and the core in tension (core about half the surface compression)
Strength: an applied tensile stress must first cancel the surface compression, so the failure stress is about annealed strength plus surface compression
Limitation: cannot be cut or drilled after tempering; stored core tension causes fragmentation; edge damage reaching the core causes spontaneous breakage
questions.explanation: Tempering relies on differential cooling through the glass transition, locking in a compressive layer. The compressive layer raises the load needed to open surface flaws, at the cost of stored elastic energy in the core.

questions.stem: Select a ceramic for (i) a wear plate in a mineral chute, (ii) a kiln support operating at 1500 C with frequent thermal cycling and (iii) a ceramic knife blade that must resist chipping. Justify each choice with reference to hardness, toughness and temperature capability, and state one limit of each.
markingGuide: (i) Wear plate: alumina (or SiC) chosen for hardness and low cost; limit: brittle, so needs mounting in compression and protection against impact

(ii) Kiln support: silicon carbide (or alumina) for high-temperature strength; SiC for high conductivity and low expansion resisting thermal shock; limit: oxidation and thermal shock, thermal expansion mismatch

(iii) Knife blade: toughened zirconia chosen for its higher toughness (transformation toughening) combined with good hardness; limit: lower hardness than SiC and loss of toughening at elevated temperature
Uses toughness K_Ic (about 3.5 to 4.5 for alumina and 6 to 10 for zirconia) and hardness values in the comparison
Mentions flaw sensitivity or scatter in strength as a general limit for all three
questions.explanation: The three components emphasise different properties: wear (hardness), temperature and thermal shock (conductivity and expansion), and impact resistance (toughness). Each selected ceramic keeps the property that matters but still shares the general limitation of brittleness and strength scatter.
